newsitem.title: USA: Brent talk growing in U.S. foreign crude market.
newsitem.headline: Brent talk growing in U.S. foreign crude market.

text.p: The market for foreign crudes into the U.S. Gulf Coast was filled Thursday with talk of a Brent cargo getting fixed, but no one could say for sure that anything was getting done, traders said.

With OPEC having concluded its business in Vienna and the market taking two volatile sessions to settle on what amounted to an indifferent reaction, traders were concentrating on the fate of the Iraqi oil-for-food deal.

They said the longer the market waits for Iraqi barrels, the more domestic grades like Light Louisiana Sweet/St James and West Texas Sour/Midland are likely to firm and the more likely foreign crudes will fetch the right price to be worked into the U.S.

The Brent-West Texas Intermediate/Cushing spread expanded by 9 cents Thursday to $1.32 a barrel, suggesting August Brent deals were growing closer to being doable if there have not yet in fact been any done this week.
A Brent cargo was again, like on Wednesday, rumored to have been sold sometime this week at August WTI/Cushing minus 35 cents, but that could not be immediately confirmed.
At least one seller, a U.S. player, was offering Brent at that price, and players said they were getting interested.
Nigerian Qua Iboe on a delivered basis was also being offered at prices around Dated Brent plus $1.82-$1.84 a barrel, traders said.
The August picture for Colombian Cusiana began to emerge amid talk Total had set a loading of a cargo of the gasoline-rich crude for August 16-20.
But neither the rest of the loading program nor the price Total might be asking had yet emerged.
But some players continued to cite the $1.00 under September WTI/Cushing fob price BP is said to have been floating earlier this week as a starting point.

That number is considered to be high by many players on the buying side of the ledger. But with domestic grades firming and talk of tightness on the Gulf Coast growing, it remained too early to tell if it really is too high, traders said.
-- Oliver Ludwig, New York Oil Desk +1 212 859 1633
